K1.text: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the **most common cyanotic congenital heart disease**. Its clinical presentation varies with the severity of **right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction**.

K2.text: TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease in children **beyond the neonatal period**

K3.text: Classic TOF has four components: a **large, anteriorly malaligned VSD**, an **overriding aorta**, **infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction** and **right ventricular hypertrophy**.

K4.text: Chest radiographs may classically show a **"boot-shaped" heart**, with an upturned apex due to right ventricular hypertrophy.

K5.text: **Pentalogy of Fallot** = TOF plus an **atrial septal defect**; the term is old and seldom used now.

K6.text: The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary diagnostic modality.

K7.text: The **22q11.2 deletion** is the most common syndromic association of TOF

K8.text: Classic TOF is a congenital heart defect comprised of 4 anatomical alterations:

K9.text: A large, **anteriorly malaligned ventricular septal defect (VSD)**.

K12.text: **Right ventricular hypertrophy**, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

K13.text: **ASD and PDA** are among the other anomalies that *may accompany* TOF; the four components listed by StatPearls and CDC include no ASD, PDA or LVH.

K14.text: StatPearls gives an incidence of 5 to 7 per 10,000 live births and a prevalence of 1 in 3,000 births.

K15.text: Garagiola and Thorne give an incidence of 3–5 per 10,000 live births, or 7–10% of all birth defects

K16.text: Gagliardi et al. give a worldwide birth prevalence of about 3 to 6 per 10,000 live births, about 7–10% of all congenital heart defects

K17.text: The **22q11.2 deletion** is the most common syndromic association, present in up to 15% of TOF cases

K18.text: In one TOF cohort, 22q11.2 deletion syndrome had a prevalence of 6%

K19.text: A **right aortic arch** is seen in 20–25% of TOF.

K20.text: With significant RVOT obstruction, most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.

K21.text: Chest radiographs can therefore show decreased pulmonary vascular markings (**pulmonary oligaemia**).

K22.text: If the resistance across the RVOT is less than the systemic vascular resistance, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.

K23.text: Infants with moderate RVOT obstruction who were not diagnosed before birth may be asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur, and may be referred to as **"pink Tets"**.

K24.text: TOF most commonly presents as a **cyanotic neonate**.

K25.text: The murmur has a **harsh systolic ejection** quality, best heard at the left mid to upper sternal border with posterior radiation.

K26.text: The greater the degree of obstruction, the more prominent the murmur.

K27.text: The pulmonic component of **S2** is usually inaudible.

K28.text: **Tet (hypercyanotic) spells** can be triggered by agitation, pain, anaemia, fever, hypovolaemia or peripheral vasodilatation.

K29.text: During a tet spell there is a **decrease in the intensity of the murmur**.

K30.text: **ECG**: right axis deviation, prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1, characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.

K31.text: **Chest X-ray**: StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex and a concave or "boot-shaped" main pulmonary artery segment.

K32.text: The upturned apex of the **boot-shaped heart** is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy, together with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.

K33.text: Most infants with TOF, however, may not show the boot-shaped finding

K34.text: **Echocardiogram**: the gold standard for the diagnosis of TOF.

K35.text: Echocardiography allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy and remains the primary modality for diagnosis.

K36.text: Echocardiography has limitations in assessing associated extracardiac anomalies, such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia

K37.text: **Contrast-enhanced CT** is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology of TOF.

K38.text: CT can evaluate post-surgical changes, such as patency of palliative shunts, and complications

K39.text: **MRI** provides both anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.

K40.text: Detailed pulmonary artery assessment matters because repairing the cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome

K41.text: The main or right pulmonary artery diameter should be compared with that of the ascending aorta

K42.text: Tet spells require a rapid and aggressive approach.

K43.text: **Knee-chest positioning**, to increase systemic vascular resistance.

K45.text: **IV fluid boluses**, to improve RV filling.

K46.text: **IV beta-blockers**, to decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further.

K48.text: **Morphine** can be given as a sedative during a tet spell.

K49.text: The timing of TOF repair is still in debate.

K50.text: StatPearls describes deferring complete surgical repair to after the first 3 months of life.

K51.text: Al Mosa et al. consider **3–6 months of age** likely the ideal time frame for elective repair, and advocate repair at 3–6 months in asymptomatic patients

K52.text: The same authors prefer primary neonatal or early repair for symptomatic infants with TOF

K53.text: The first surgical treatment of TOF was a palliative subclavian-to-pulmonary-artery shunt by Blalock and Taussig

K54.text: The **Blalock-Taussig shunt** connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.

K55.text: Al Mosa et al. reserve staging with initial palliation for infants with high-risk features: low birth weight or prematurity, and small or discontinuous pulmonary arteries

K56.text: They do not palliate patients who present as neonates without high-risk features

K57.text: Drawbacks include the limited lifespan of the shunt and an increased incidence of late sudden death

K58.text: Morbidities of initial palliation include pulmonary artery stenosis and distortion, and smaller pulmonary arteries before repair

K59.text: Pulmonary valve replacement can be achieved surgically or by a transcatheter approach.

K60.text: **Pulmonary regurgitation** results from reconstruction of the RVOT.

K61.text: **Pulmonary insufficiency** is the most common indication for reoperation.

K62.text: Arrhythmias can occur after TOF repair, including **ventricular tachycardia**.

K63.text: 40–50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias.

K64.text: The risk of sudden death is 6–9% 30 years after the surgical procedure.

K65.text: The most frequent causes of mortality without surgical intervention include **hypoxic spells (68%)**.

K66.text: Cerebrovascular accidents (17%) and brain abscesses (13%) are also listed among the causes of mortality without surgery.

K67.text: Chronic hypoxaemia can cause hyperviscosity, abnormal haemostasis, stroke, **cerebral abscess** and endocarditis.

K68.text: Patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of **endocarditis**.

K75.text: PYQs have expected TOF as the most common cyanotic CHD beyond the neonatal period, as Garagiola and Thorne state; current StatPearls says TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.

K76.text: PYQs have expected pentalogy of Fallot = TOF + atrial septal defect; CDC confirms this and calls it an old term seldom used now.

K77.text: PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as "not part of TOF"; current StatPearls lists the four components as a VSD, an overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.

K78.text: PYQs have keyed the boot-shaped heart to TOF; Radiopaedia says most infants with TOF may not show this finding

K79.text: Sources differ on 22q11.2 deletion frequency: up to 15% of TOF cases versus 6% in one TOF cohort.

K80.text: Sources differ on frequency: 5 to 7 per 10,000 live births in StatPearls, 3–5 per 10,000 in Garagiola and Thorne, and about 3 to 6 per 10,000 in Gagliardi et al..
